speaker: Essa
text: Sixteen years ago. The hard winter — the one they still talk about.

speaker: Essa
text: Your father was checking snares at the forest edge. And he heard—

speaker: Tam
text: Crying. Out of the cold, at the old beech. A baby, wrapped up warm as bread from the oven. Alone.

speaker: Essa
text: No note. No name. No tracks in the snow — none, Kai. And laid beside the basket, like it was standing guard…
She cannot finish. She looks at his father. His father does not move.

speaker: Kai
text: …What. Laid beside the basket — what?
The silence stretches.

speaker: Kai
text: Sixteen years. You let me think— every time I asked why I don't have Ma's eyes, you laughed and changed the—

speaker: Essa
text: Because we were afraid! Not of you — never of you. Afraid you'd feel less ours. Afraid whoever left you would come back. Afraid of exactly this day — and look, here it is, come anyway.

speaker: Essa
text: We kept telling ourselves: next year. When he's older. Sixteen next-years, Kai. That's my fault to carry, not yours.
His father leaves the room. No word. Something in Kai's face breaks a little more.

speaker: Kai
text: …He can't even sit through it.

His father comes back. In his arms: a long bundle, oilcloth, tied with cord gone soft from years of knotting and unknotting. He sets it on the table like it weighs more than it does — and unwraps a sword. Plain scabbard. Old fittings. Not a spot of rust anywhere.

speaker: Tam
text: Every winter. Oiled it, checked the edge, wrapped it back up. Sixteen winters.

speaker: Tam
text: Never let your mother watch. Felt like… if nobody saw it, it wasn't quite real yet. And you were still just ours.

Kai reaches out. The moment his fingers touch the grip — a flicker of faint green runs the length of the blade. Like a door waking. His parents go very still: sixteen winters, and it never once did THAT.

speaker: Kai
text: It's… warm.

speaker: Tam
text: It was yours before you were ours. We kept it safe. Same as we kept you.

speaker: Essa
text: You were never less ours, Kai. Not for one single day. Whatever that light is. Whoever's coming down that road.
Kai looks at the sword. The green light dies down, patient. Then he sets it down — and takes their hands instead, both of them, hard.

speaker: Kai
text: I'm still angry. I think I'm going to be angry for a while. …Don't let go anyway.
The sword waited. It was good at that. It had already waited sixteen years — and it was, after all, the least important thing his parents gave him that night.
A fist on the door. Three knocks. Unhurried. The kind of knock that has never once been refused.
